A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same WaTL/AWaTL research, with matching authors, core algorithms, and shared experiments. All supplied pages, figures, equations, and appendices were readable, allowing the retained content and additional appendix material to be compared.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulations, source-selection experiments, NHANES physical-activity predictions, and human-mortality results.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds mortality comparisons, target-sample-size results, and training-time measurements.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–2 retain the same aggregation, bias correction, source selection, and projection. Algorithms 3–6 explicitly document local weighting and empirical-measure substitution already described in v1 Section 3.1 and its conclusion; their additional detail does not establish a changed underlying procedure.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same synthetic distribution-regression setting, NHANES 2005–2006 populations, and 2015 mortality data from 162 countries. The smaller mortality sample sizes remain within existing dataset and task coverage.

E2.justification: The mortality comparison expands substantially from WaTL versus target-only Fréchet regression to target-only, source-only, and pooled-data baselines using both Fréchet regression and Wasserstein Regression (Chen et al., 2023). Figure 3(b) confirms their evaluated participation. Source-only regression was already evaluated in simulations, but is newly included in the mortality comparison.

E3.justification: Table 1 introduces mortality evaluations with 14 and 19 target samples alongside the existing 24-sample setting, plus training time as an additional measure. The simulation and NHANES protocols remain unchanged. Removing v1's statement that mortality evaluation used no cross-validation does not establish that cross-validation was introduced.

E4.justification: v2 adds a mortality analysis testing sensitivity to target-data scarcity and measuring training time in Table 1. The existing negative-transfer ablation, adaptive source-selection analysis, and NHANES prediction examples are retained.

E5.justification: The stated 50 simulation repetitions and 100 source-selection repetitions are unchanged. v2 adds no seed information, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty estimates; the new mortality table reports point values only.

E6.justification: The mortality results are expanded and revised: v2 reports WaTL RMSPR of 0.022 versus target-only Fréchet and Wasserstein regression values of 0.027 and 0.025. Table 1 adds RMSPR values 0.028, 0.025, and 0.022 and training times 0.598, 0.597, and 0.694 ms for 14, 19, and 24 target samples. Figures 1–2 are unchanged. These are newly reported results, not established same-setting improvements over v1.

T1.justification: v1 states Lemma 1 and Theorems 1–3 without supplying their proofs. v2 adds proofs, quantile-measurability and general-metric-space lemmas, additional assumptions, and Theorems 4–7 covering local regression and empirical measures. These introduce substantive bandwidth- and within-distribution-sample-size-dependent guarantees, while the main theorem statements remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central claims: a Wasserstein transfer-learning framework, adaptive informative-source selection, convergence guarantees, and improved target estimation. The additional appendix evidence does not materially redefine those contributions.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the mortality pooling results as evidence for the necessity of bias correction and the new table as evidence of robustness to scarce target data and computational practicality. v1 offered a more general cross-population transfer interpretation. The fully observed-distribution limitation was already acknowledged in v1.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-availability link, explicit local and empirical-measure pseudocode, further tuning guidance, and training-time information. However, it removes the mortality study's population-density/GDP covariate specification and explicit no-cross-validation disclosure. Hardware and subsample-selection details remain unspecified.

R1.justification: v2 adds supporting references including Bobkov and Ledoux, Iao et al., van der Vaart, Vershynin, Wainwright, and Zhou et al.'s model-assisted transfer regression. These mainly support the new appendices; the related-work narrative and claimed research gap remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: Most main-text prose and section ordering are retained with limited editing. The mortality discussion is rewritten, references move before the appendices, the empirical-measure limitation moves from the conclusion to the theory discussion, and acknowledgments are added. The added scientific appendices do not constitute a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: Figure 3(b) is redrawn with grouped comparator bars and a regression-method legend; Table 1 and additional algorithm displays are added. Narrower text columns reflow the document and resize retained figures. Figures 1–2 and the mortality-density panel preserve their content, while Figure 3's caption still describes only WaTL and Only Target.

improvement.justification: v2 improves inspectability through explicit proofs, algorithm documentation, code-access information, and stronger mortality controls. However, the new Lemma 2 proof incorrectly equates a set over all quantile arguments with a union of rational slices, and Theorem 7 omits the h^4 local-bias term retained in Theorem 4 without justification. Mortality covariate and evaluation disclosures also disappear. These concrete theoretical and reproducibility concerns prevent a reliable judgment of the net quality improvement.
